details:
WHAT IT DOES
Lunar Site Navigator is a free web app that answers a mission planner's key question in seconds: if we land at this lunar south-pole site on this date, or the launch slips, will we still have sunlight for power and Earth in view for a direct radio link?


Near the south pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° and Earth hangs low and wobbles (libration), so a single hill, a few hundred metres or a few days can decide whether a lander has power and contact. For any site and date the app shows the real Sun and Earth over the real terrain horizon and turns that geometry into clear metrics: share of time in sunlight, share of time with Earth in view, the longest night, the longest communication blackout, and a transparent 0–100 score.
Main features:
- Mission Rescue: when a launch slips, it re-ranks every candidate site on every nearby day and proposes the three best options, each with a score and a one-line reason.
- Sky view: a 360° horizon panorama with the Sun and Earth paths, a time slider, and plain-language summaries.
- 3D south-pole terrain lit by the real Sun, with lines of sight from each site to the Sun and Earth (red where a hill blocks them), plus monthly light and signal maps for the whole region.
- Landing precision: scores 250 m and 1 km off target, because landers miss (IM-1 Odysseus landed about 1.5 km away). Shackleton rim falls from 71 to 1 just 250 m off the crest.
- Who else is here: hardware already on the surface and planned missions near each site, with a 2 km plume safety zone.
- A battery model of a reference lander, a 12-month calendar of the best launch windows, side-by-side comparison, PDF reports and shareable links.
HOW IT WORKS
For each site we compute a terrain horizon from NASA LRO LOLA polar elevation models (20, 40, 80 and 240 m per pixel): 1440 rays out to 200 km, including the Moon's curvature. Sun and Earth positions come from astronomy-engine, converted into the Moon's body-fixed frame with the IAU rotation model and libration. There is no atmosphere, so there is no refraction. We model the partial solar disk and require Earth to clear the hills by 2° for a reliable link.
VALIDATION
- 130 comparisons with NASA JPL Horizons: maximum error 0.004° (target 0.1°).
- Annual illumination: Connecting Ridge 85.4% vs 88.0% and Shackleton rim 84.3% vs 82.1% published by Gläser et al. (NASA); the permanently shadowed Shackleton floor gets 0%.
- 44 automated tests; the full comparison is public on the Validation page.
BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Mission planners can re-plan a slipped launch in seconds instead of re-running a full analysis. Scientists get exact angles, azimuths and CSV exports. Students and the public get a Simple mode, a 30-second guided tour and a 3D view that show why landing near the pole is so hard. The app is free, open source and runs in any browser, including phones, with no installation and no server costs.
TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES
TypeScript, Next.js and React, Tailwind CSS, three.js (WebGL) for 3D, Web Workers for parallel map computation, Python for the terrain pipeline, Vitest for tests, Vercel for hosting. Data: NASA LRO LOLA, NASA JPL Horizons API, LROC and NASA SVS imagery, NASA Blue Marble, LRO Diviner, plus partner data from KARI (ShadowCam), JAXA (Kaguya) and ISRO (Chandrayaan). Code and documentation were largely written with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code by Anthropic) under the team's specification; every number is verified against NASA data.
CREATIVITY
Most tools answer either "where" or "when". We combine both with the things that decide a real mission: landing accuracy, neighbouring missions, battery survival and launch slips. Everything runs in the browser, so answers are instant and shareable as a link, and the same numbers serve engineers and the public through two interface modes.
FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific accuracy first: real terrain instead of a flat horizon, lunar curvature, libration, the Sun's partial disk and independent validation. We were honest about limits: approximate results are labelled, and we do not yet model relay satellites, thermal conditions or slopes. We also considered plume safety around existing hardware, landing error, accessibility for non-experts, and openness: free, no login, all sources cited.
